 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Semi smuggling:  Nvidia's ( NVDA ) Jensen is out and banned chips traced to Alice Huang-linked firm .

 Strategic decoupling: China is reportedly looking to build a rival to insure global shipping .

 AI frenzy: Anthropic's ( ANT ) IPO is six times oversubscribed , with debut set for next week.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Two catches 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 SpaceX ( SPCX ) has already revolutionized spaceflight, but it keeps testing the final frontier. It was only a decade ago that the company successfully demonstrated the viability of reusable rocket boosters, leading it to become the dominant player in the industry. Those have continued with Falcon 9 (via drone ships and ground pads) and Starship (via launch tower chopsticks), but the time has come to take it a step further. SpaceX and Tesla could merge as soon as December 

 Back to Earth: Up until now, reusable rocket initiatives have focused on first-stage boosters. Those are the massive lower sections packed with engines and fuel that do the heavy lifting to push the rocket through the thickest part of the atmosphere. Not much attention was given to reusing the second stage, which carries cargo, including satellites and crew, to orbit—until now.

The reason was economic. To recover a Falcon 9 second stage, a heavy heat shield would need to be added, along with landing legs, grid fins, and extra landing fuel. That would have cut into payload capacity, especially when the second stage is relatively inexpensive compared to the booster. The economics are way different for the Starship, whose enormous size and cargo capacity make it cost-effective to add all those items .

 Get ready: With a launch window of 5:45 PM to 7:00 PM ET, SpaceX ( SPCX ) this evening will attempt a mission it has never done before: recovering an entire rocket launched into space. Recapturing both the first stage (minutes after liftoff) and second stage (on Saturday afternoon) would herald an era of full launch vehicle reusability and "unlock the true capability of Starship." SpaceX hopes the next-generation system will eventually replace its entire Falcon rocket fleet for commercial satellite launches or International Space Station missions. It would also power Elon Musk's long-term vision of lunar landings, point-to-point Earth transport, and, of course, colonizing Mars.
